links.outcome: Patient intent to consent under brief vs expanded ambient AI disclosure language
links.effect: 84 patients (81.6%) consented with basic information vs 57 (55.3%) when AI features, data storage, and corporate involvement were disclosed; yet 96.1%-98.1% rated data-use details important.
links.quote: When provided basic information about the technology ( Figure , A), 84 patients (81.6%) consented; this decreased to 57 patients (55.3%) when details about AI features, data storage, and corporate involvement were disclosed ( Figure , B).

links.outcome: Stated willingness to consent under basic versus expanded technology and data-use disclosures
links.effect: Consent was 84 patients (81.6%) with basic information versus 57 patients (55.3%) after disclosure of AI features, data storage, and corporate involvement; comprehension was not measured.
links.quote: When provided basic information about the technology ( Figure , A), 84 patients (81.6%) consented; this decreased to 57 patients (55.3%) when details about AI features, data storage, and corporate involvement were disclosed ( Figure , B).

links.outcome: Clinician-reported barriers to explaining ambient AI during consent
links.effect: Clinicians reported time constraints, concerns about biased presentation, and uncertainty about which details to disclose; frequencies were not quantified.
links.quote: Clinicians cited time constraints, concerns about bias in presenting the technology, and uncertainty about what details to include ( Box 3 ).

links.outcome: Patient-reported anticipated self-censorship during sensitive discussions with ambient documentation
links.effect: Patients reported anticipated self-censorship when discussing mental health (36 [35.0%]), sexual health (42 [40.8%]), or illicit activity (53 [51.5%]).
links.quote: However, patients were more likely to censor what they said when discussing mental health (36 [35.0%]), sexual health (42 [40.8%]), or illicit activity (53 [51.5%]).
